paragraphs: Upakosala Kamalayana was a student of Satyakama, the boy from the previous story who had grown into a teacher himself. Upakosala lived with his Guru for a time, learning from him.
Then Satyakama left on a journey, and the young disciple sank into gloom. When his teacher's wife noticed he had stopped eating and asked what was wrong, he told her he was simply too unhappy to eat.

Just then a voice rose from the fire he tended. Life is Brahman, it said; Brahman is the ether, Brahman is happiness; know Brahman. Upakosala answered that he understood life to be Brahman, but how could It be ether and happiness? The voice explained that both words point to one reality: the pure, conscious intelligence that dwells in the heart.

The fire went on teaching him. The earth, food, fire and the sun that he worshipped were all forms of Brahman. The Being seen in the sun, in the directions, the moon, the stars and the water, in life, the sky and the lightning: "I am He," said the voice. Whoever knows and meditates on this is freed from sin, lives long and becomes happy.

Swamiji pointed out what makes this practical religion. The voice never told Upakosala that the fire, sun or moon he worshipped were wrong or unreal. Instead it showed him that the same spirit living in all of them also lived in him. The fire was no longer just flames for offerings; it became the Lord. Earth, sun, moon, lightning and life itself were seen in a new light, their true nature revealed.
This, Swamiji said, is Vedanta's real gift. It does not tear down the world or the individual; it explains them, so that the world, once understood, can no longer hurt you.
learn: You don't have to run away from ordinary life to find meaning; the deeper reality is right inside the familiar things around you. Even a low moment, like Upakosala's, can become the doorway to a bigger understanding if you stay open.
